problem: Target-driven visual navigation policies that learn directly from visual or semantic feature values generalize poorly to unseen scenes and objects. This is especially true when the target is not visible at first, or when new instances or slightly different object classes appear.
motivation: Humans search for an object by looking at the surrounding context objects: they head to where the target is likely to be, then go straight to it once it is visible. Visual and semantic features change whenever new objects or instances are introduced, so a representation that encodes only how much each location resembles the target should transfer better to unseen scenes and objects.
key_idea: Convert the egocentric observation into a 'context grid': a spatial map whose cell values give the semantic similarity between the object at that location and the target object. The navigation policy is learned on this grid instead of on raw visual or semantic features.
insight: The context grid stores relative similarity to the target rather than raw appearance or semantic feature values. The policy input therefore stays stable when new instances or nearby classes appear, which, per the authors, is why it generalizes to unseen scenes and objects. The same representation supports two-phase behavior: context-guided exploration while the target is unseen, then fast approach once it is visible. The abstract describes no ablations, so these claims cannot be checked against specific ablation results.
method: Context grid: an intermediate spatial representation built from detected objects in the current view, where each cell encodes how semantically similar the object at that location is to the target. The abstract does not state the exact detector or similarity measure; object detection plus word-embedding similarity is likely.
Joint target/context encoding: the target object and the other scene objects are encoded in the same grid, so the policy can use context objects when the target is not in view.

Learned navigation policy: a navigation model trained on the context grid to output actions that reach the target object. The abstract does not name the RL algorithm; an actor-critic method (e.g., A3C) is likely.
Human performance study: human subjects performed the same target-driven navigation task, and their results were compared with learning-based approaches including this one.

setting.backbone: Not stated in abstract. Likely a learned navigation policy network on top of a pretrained object detector and word embeddings that form the context grid.
setting.training_data: Not stated in abstract. Likely trained with RL in indoor simulated scenes (AI2-THOR-style room scenes).
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB, converted into a context grid (object locations × semantic similarity to the target)
setting.action_space: Not stated in abstract (likely discrete move/rotate actions)

results: The authors report that the context-grid approach outperforms previous approaches when navigating in unseen scenes, with the largest gains in broad (large) scenes. They also compare against human performance on the same target-driven navigation task. The abstract gives no numeric results.
limitations: The context grid depends on the quality of object detection and of the semantic-similarity measure; missed or misclassified objects corrupt the representation.
Only a single egocentric context grid is described, with no explicit long-term memory or map, which may limit search in multi-room or large environments.
Evaluation appears to be simulation-only; the abstract reports no real-robot results.
compares_to: Semantic/scene-prior based navigation (e.g., Yang et al., 2019)
